result: Mettl3-CKO retinas exhibit structural and functional abnormalities beginning at the end of retinogenesis. At p0, retinas appeared grossly normal, but by p14, they showed severe structural disorganization with rosette formations in the ONL, displaced INL cells, disrupted OLM, and abnormal Müller cell morphology. Visual function was also disrupted as measured by mfERG.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the study 'clearly demonstrated the defects of Mettl3CKO retina in mice, including cellular disorganization and abnormal physiological responses.' The structural and functional phenotypes are well-documented with histology, immunofluorescence, and electrophysiology data.

result: Mettl3 deficiency affects late but not early RPC proliferation and cell cycle progression. At E15.5, BrdU+ cell numbers were similar between mutant and control, but at p1, fewer BrdU+ cells were observed in Mettl3-CKO retinas. Cell cycle progression was prolonged (S-to-M phase) and cell cycle withdrawal was delayed in late RPCs. In vivo electroporation of shRNAs targeting Mettl3 confirmed these effects.
evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about data consistency. Reviewer 1 noted that 'fewer BrdU+ cells at P1 (2 hours after BrdU injection) in cko' does not necessarily support slower proliferation, and questioned whether 'cko RPCs withdrew from the cell cycle slower than control RPCs' is consistent with having 'significantly less BrdU+ cells at P1.' The reviewers requested clarification of these apparent contradictions.

result: Cell type composition changes in Mettl3-CKO retinas at p7 include increased SOX9+ Müller glia, unchanged VSX2+ bipolar cells, reduced RHODOPSIN+ photoreceptors, and reduced CALBINDIN+ horizontal cells. Other cell types (RGCs, amacrine cells, cones) were comparable to controls.
evaluation: Reviewers identified inconsistencies between different datasets. Reviewer 2 noted that 'in Mettl3CKO mice, the author found an increased number of Müller glia...However, in the retinae with the overexpression of Zfp292, Ckap4, Traf4, or Bcl7a, they found an increase in the percentage of Müller cells at the expense of amacrine cells or rod photoreceptors.' Additionally, 'in scRNAseq data analysis, only the proportion of RPCs increased, but not Müller glial cells...This result is not consistent with the IF phenotype.' Reviewers requested clarification of these discrepancies.

result: Apoptosis is significantly elevated in Mettl3-CKO retinas, affecting both RPCs and differentiated cells. This leads to severe degeneration of all cellular layers at older ages and may contribute to reduced photoreceptor and BrdU+ cell populations.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted that 'the authors showed that there are significant cell death in the cko retinas at P0, P6 and P14...But they didn't show which types of cells are dying. Many TUNEL positive cells are in ONL.' The reviewer also stated 'This cell death was also not carefully integrated into their conclusions when they explained the phenotypes or results.' The contribution of cell death to the observed phenotypes requires better integration and clarification.

result: scRNA-seq analysis at p7 revealed transcriptomic changes in Mettl3-CKO retinas. Cells clustered into nine clusters representing typical retinal cell types. The proportion of RPCs was nearly twofold higher in mutants, while rod proportion was slightly reduced. Pseudotime analysis showed delayed gliogenesis progression in Mettl3-CKO RPCs.
evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about data consistency and interpretation. Reviewer 1 noted that 'at P7, based on their single cell RNA-seq data, 6% of retinal cells were RPCs in control retinas, and 11% of retinal cells were RPCs in Mettl3cko...However, the number seems to be very high for control P7 retinas. In published single cell datasets (Clark et al. 2019), the percentage of retinal cells identified as RPCs was close to 0 at around P7.' Additionally, 'in Figure 3—figure supplement 3, the authors stained P7 Mettl3cko and control retinas with Ki67. There was a very limited number of Ki67+ cells in Mettl3cko, which doesn't quite match the 11% found in single cell RNA-seq data.' These inconsistencies need resolution.

result: Reclustering and DEG analysis revealed that RPCs and Müller cells are the two cell types most affected by Mettl3 deficiency. In mutant RPCs, 286 genes were upregulated (enriched for gene expression regulation) and 212 downregulated (enriched for organelle, metabolism, cell cycle regulation). In mutant Müller cells, 239 genes were upregulated (enriched for RPC-associated transcription factors) and 181 downregulated (enriched for cell shape, actin filament organization, and glycolytic processes).
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged that 'Enriched scRNA-seq and MeRIP-seq data provide excellent resources to study the function of m6A modification in retinogenesis.' The detailed transcriptomic analysis of RPCs and Müller cells is well-supported by the data, though reviewers requested additional discussion of how these findings relate to the overall phenotype.

result: MeRIP-seq analysis identified the retinal m6A epitranscriptome at p0, p7, and adult stages. The m6A peaks were localized in the CDS region with enrichment around stop codons and the GGACU motif. The m6A epitranscriptome was enriched for genes involved in retinal development, structural organization, and visual function.
evaluation: Reviewers noted that 'Enriched scRNA-seq and MeRIP-seq data provide excellent resources to study the function of m6A modification in retinogenesis.' The MeRIP-seq characterization is comprehensive and well-documented. However, Reviewer 1 noted that 'The stage of the retina was not consistent across experiments. The single cell RNA-seq experiment was performed using P7 retinas, whereas MeRIP-seq used P6 retinas. Twenty-four hours could make a big difference in terms of transcription at this stage.'

result: Integrative analysis of scRNA-seq and MeRIP-seq data demonstrated that m6A modification promotes degradation of RPC transcripts during the RPC-to-Müller transition. m6A-tagged transcripts were upregulated in Mettl3-mutant RPC and Müller glia clusters. Analysis of intermediate cell states showed that m6A-RPC transcripts failed to be promptly downregulated during the transition.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the integrative analysis approach. The detailed analysis of intermediate cell states and m6A-tagged gene expression patterns provides strong support for the proposed mechanism. This represents a key mechanistic finding of the study.

result: Validation experiments showed that m6A modification levels and transcript half-lives of candidate genes (Zfp292, Ckap4, Traf4, Bcl7a) were altered in Mettl3-CKO retinas. Overexpression of these genes in late RPCs prohibited cell cycle exit and biased cells toward Müller glial fate at the expense of neurons.
evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about the interpretation of these experiments. Reviewer 1 stated that 'the authors over-expressed candidate m6A-regulated genes in RPCs and showed that they prevented the RPCs from exiting the cell cycle. However, the data presented in Figure 6 cannot fully support this conclusion. PCNA is not a pan cell cycle marker. Reduction of GFP+PCNA- cells in Mettl3cko doesn't necessarily mean that mutant cells failed to exit the cell cycle.' Additionally, Reviewer 2 noted inconsistencies between the overexpression phenotype and the Mettl3-CKO phenotype regarding cell type composition changes.

result: Dysfunction of Müller glial cells is proposed as the cellular basis for retinal structural abnormalities in Mettl3-CKO retinas. Evidence includes timing of phenotype appearance coinciding with Müller glia maturation, severe transcriptomic changes in Müller cells, and downregulation of genes involved in cell-cell interaction and cytoskeleton.
evaluation: Reviewers questioned whether the structural abnormalities are direct effects of Müller glial defects or secondary effects. Reviewer 1 stated: 'The authors showed disrupted retina structure in Mettl3cko and claimed that dysfunction of Muller glial cells was the underlying cause. However, based on the data presented in the manuscript, it is not clear whether retinal structure abnormalities are direct effects of Muller glial defects or secondary effects induced by defects in RPCs or other cell types.' Reviewer 1 also noted 'The authors claim that Mettl3cko "…compromises the function of Muller cells" (abstract line 32). There is no direct evidence to support this point.'

result: The regulatory function of Mettl3 during retinal development is restricted to late-stage retinogenesis. Despite Six3-Cre expression from E9.5, retinas remained normal until the postnatal period. In vivo electroporation experiments directly targeting late RPCs confirmed Mettl3's requirement in late RPCs.
evaluation: Reviewers initially requested direct testing of Mettl3's role in late RPCs. The authors addressed this with in vivo electroporation experiments. Reviewer 2 noted in the second round: 'the new data of shRNA targeting Mettl3 expressed in late RPCs directly addressed the cell-type specificity of Mettl3's role.' However, Reviewer 1 noted that 'For all the shRNA-based experiments, there aren't any control experiments to show their efficiency and specificity.'

result: Background claims about m6A modification, retinal biology, and the knowledge gap regarding m6A function in the visual system.
evaluation: These are established background facts cited from the literature. Reviewers did not question these claims. However, Reviewer 2 noted: 'I am surprised that the authors did not provide the background of previous studies of m6A in retinal development. Adding these research backgrounds will further improve the clarity of this study by putting it into context.'

result: Discussion of broader implications and comparison to m6A function in other neural tissues, particularly cortical development. The study suggests conservation of some m6A regulatory mechanisms between NSCs and RPCs, and speculates about potential applicability to other nervous systems.
evaluation: Reviewers requested better contextualization with previous m6A studies in neural development. Reviewer 1 stated: 'The role of m6A on neural development has been extensively studied in the brain. The authors did not discuss these published papers and did not explain how their work improved the field.' The authors addressed this in revision by adding discussion of cortical development studies, which reviewers found satisfactory.
